planting.note: Nick or lightly scarify the hard seed coat and direct sow into pure, loose, bare sand in full sun, since this pioneer species needs open, unvegetated ground to establish and will not compete in a planted bed.

directions: Pickering's dawnflower is a trailing, deep-rooted perennial vine of the open, deep-sand longleaf pine sandhills of the North and South Carolina fall line, where it threads across bare, loose sand between wiregrass clumps rather than climbing. Its silky-haired, narrow leaves and funnel-shaped white flowers, marked with a pale lavender or pink throat and opening only in morning sun, closely resemble a miniature bindweed. Give it the sharpest possible drainage and the leanest, most mineral sand you can provide, since any organic enrichment or shade from encroaching groundcover quickly causes it to decline. Because its taproot runs deep almost immediately, start it in place from seed or small plugs rather than attempting to move established plants.

planting.note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall into pure, infertile, deep sand in full sun and expect slow, erratic germination, since this species relies on a massive woody taproot that takes years to fully establish and makes transplanting all but impossible.

directions: Carolina ipecac is a low, sprawling spurge endemic to the deep, droughty sands of the Carolina sandhills and inner coastal plain, sending up a handful of prostrate to ascending stems from an enormous, carrot-like taproot that can store years of reserves against drought and fire. Its paired leaves vary from plain green to shades flushed with red or maroon, and small yellow-green flower clusters called cyathia appear from late winter into spring, well before most sandhill wildflowers wake up. It wants nothing but lean, sharply drained sand and full sun, and will rot quickly in any soil that holds moisture or receives supplemental irrigation. Treat it as a permanent, slow-to-establish specimen for a dedicated xeric sand garden rather than a plant to be divided or moved once settled.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into bare, loose, acidic sand in full sun, where winter chilling helps break dormancy; this is a true deep-sand pioneer and will not establish in mulched or vegetated ground.

directions: Carolina sandwort, long known in older references as Arenaria caroliniana, is a wiry, mat-forming perennial that is frequent to common across the North and South Carolina sandhills but becomes scarce outside this deep-sand fall-line belt. Thread-like, needle-fine leaves cluster densely along the stems, and in spring the plant is studded with small, five-petaled white flowers held just above the sand on short, nearly leafless stalks. It depends entirely on bare, loose, mineral sand kept open by fire or erosion, and will be smothered by leaf litter, mulch, or competing turf in an ordinary garden bed. Use it as a specialty groundcover in a sand-bed or rock-garden setting with other sandhill pioneers, giving it full sun and no supplemental watering once established.
sources: Vascular Plants of North Carolina (NC State Parks)

planting.note: Scatter the tiny seeds over bare, open sand in spring and press in lightly, since this diminutive wireplant needs exposed mineral soil and full sun to compete and will disappear from any site that closes in with other vegetation.

directions: Pineland scalypink is a minute, almost lichen-like perennial of the open, xeric sandhill scrub, forming a tight basal rosette of tiny scale-edged leaves from which wiry, nearly leafless flowering stems rise and fork repeatedly into a fine, see-through haze. From May through August each branch tip opens a scattering of pinhead-sized white flowers that are easy to overlook individually but create a soft sparkle across bare sand in quantity. It is common in the Carolina sandhills precisely because it thrives on the open, bare patches between wiregrass tussocks that most other plants cannot colonize, so give it full sun and undisturbed, unmulched sand rather than a conventional bed. Let plants reseed freely in open sandy gaps, since scalypink behaves as a short-lived colonizer that persists by continually resettling bare ground.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (UNC Herbarium)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into lean, infertile, deep sand in full sun; this woody-based wildflower needs the same bare, unirrigated conditions as its sandhill neighbors and resents enriched garden soil.

directions: Southern jointweed is a woody-based perennial of the Carolina sandhills and surrounding dry coastal plain, sending up a loose cluster of slender, jointed, wiry stems from a semi-woody base each year. Small, narrow leaves are shed early, leaving the plant's airy structure of reddish, bamboo-like jointed stems to carry small white to pink flowers in loose, open sprays from late summer into fall, a season when most other sandhill wildflowers have already finished. It is a reliable late nectar source for small bees and skippers on the open, bare sand where it grows alongside wiregrass and turkey oak, and it is intolerant of shade, rich soil, or regular watering. Grow it in a dedicated dry sand bed in full sun, cutting the previous year's dried stems back in late winter to make way for new growth.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (UNC Herbarium)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plugs in spring into lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; clumps spread slowly from short rhizomes and resent heavy, wet, or richly amended ground.

directions: Piedmont roseling, also sold under its older names Cuthbertia rosea or Tradescantia rosea, is a grass-leaved perennial in the spiderwort family that forms neat, narrow-leaved tufts in the open longleaf pine sandhills of the Carolinas and Georgia. From late spring through summer it sends up slender stalks bearing clusters of small, three-petaled, rose-pink flowers that open in the morning and close by early afternoon, renewing in succession over many weeks. It is most common on the South Carolina side of the sandhills and uncommon farther north, favoring the same deep, sharply drained sand and open, fire-maintained conditions as its longleaf pine and wiregrass neighbors. Grow it in full sun in a dry, sandy bed, dividing established clumps in spring if a larger drift is wanted.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (UNC Herbarium)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or plant nursery-grown divisions in lean, deep sand in full sun; this slow-growing rosette plant can take several seasons from seed to its first flowering spike.

directions: Georgia beargrass forms a low, grass-like rosette of tough, strap-shaped evergreen leaves anchored by a thick, woody underground caudex, a growth habit that lets it resprout reliably after the frequent fires of its native turkey oak sandhill habitat. In summer, mature plants send up a tall, slender flowering stalk well above the foliage mound, carrying dense clusters of small whitish flowers that give it the alternate name sandhill lily even though it is actually in the asparagus family alongside other Nolina species. It demands the same lean, deep, sharply drained sand as its longleaf pine sandhill neighbors and is slow to establish, taking several years to reach flowering size from seed. Once settled it is extremely drought-tolerant and essentially maintenance-free, making a striking architectural accent for a xeric sand garden in full sun.

planting.note: Nick the hard seed coat and direct sow in spring into lean, deep, sandy soil in full sun; established clumps resent being dug or moved thanks to a woody taproot.

directions: Dollarleaf is a low, wiry perennial legume characteristic of the recently burned, open longleaf pine-wiregrass sandhills of the Carolina coastal plain, where it is one of the more frequently encountered small herbs on bare, deep sand. Its rounded to kidney-shaped leaflets, wider than they are long and dotted with tiny amber glands, lie close to the ground along trailing stems, and small yellow pea-like flowers appear in the leaf axils through the warm season. Like many sandhill legumes it fixes its own nitrogen and actually performs best in poor, unimproved sand, declining in richer or more regularly watered garden soil. Grow it in full sun as a low filler between larger sandhill wildflowers and grasses, and avoid mulching over the crown.
sources: Vascular Plants of North Carolina (NC State Parks)
Flora of the Southeastern United States (UNC Herbarium)

planting.note: Direct sow in spring into lean, loose, deep sand in full sun; this low subshrub needs bare, disturbed or open sandy ground and struggles where other vegetation has closed in.

directions: Sand rushfoil is a low, bushy, short-lived perennial subshrub of the open, deep-sand longleaf pine sandhills from southeastern North Carolina south into the Gulf states, recognizable by its narrow, silvery-scaled leaves that give the whole plant a pale, grayish cast. Inconspicuous greenish flowers are produced through summer on short spikes in the upper leaf axils, and the plant's modest size and silvery foliage make it more valuable as a textural accent than a showy bloomer. It colonizes the bare, disturbed or regularly burned patches of sand between wiregrass and turkey oak, and like most sandhill specialists it will decline quickly in shaded, rich, or consistently moist garden conditions. Grow it in full sun in pure sand or a xeric mineral mix, and expect individual plants to be relatively short-lived but to self-sow readily on open ground.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (UNC Herbarium)
Vascular Plants of North Carolina (NC State Parks)
